blocks.text: Who has made the cranes carry stones as ballast, which they hold in their throats against the onslaughts of the winds that are upon the earth? They wrongly read ἀμβολάς [ambolas]. For this is taken from these words of Aelian: Λίθον δὲ ἑκάστη καταπιοῦσα, ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα, πειρῶνται τοῦ μετοικισμοῦ· [Lithon de hekastē katapiousa, hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma, peirōntai tou metoikismou] Each one, having swallowed a stone to serve both as a meal and as ballast against the onslaughts of the winds, sets out on its migration. Others keep saying that this stone is a touchstone for gold. The same Aelian, book 3, chapter 13: Γέρανος δὲ λίθον ὅνπερ οὖν καταπίνει πετομένη ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔχειν ἕρμα, χρυσοῦ βάσανός ἐστιν· [Geranos de lithon honper oun katapinei petomenē hyper tou echein herma, chrysou basanos estin] The stone which the crane swallows as ballast when about to fly is a touchstone for gold. Accordingly Philes calls them

Λίθους κριτικὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ τοῖς ἐμπόροις [Lithous kritikas tou chrysou tois emporois], [II, 621] stones that test gold for merchants. But Aristotle refutes this fiction as follows, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Τὸ δὲ περὶ τοῦ λίθου ψεῦδός ἐστι· λέγεται γὰρ ὡς ἔχουσιν ἕρμα λίθον, ὃς γίνεται χρήσιμος πρὸς τὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ βασάνους, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ. [To de peri tou lithou pseudos esti; legetai gar hōs echousin herma lithon, hos ginetai chrēsimos pros tas tou chrysou basanous, hotan ekpesē.] What they tell about the stone is false: namely, that they carry a stone as ballast which, when it has fallen out, is useful for testing gold. But if this is a fiction, perhaps what follows now will be truer.

There is among them a wonderful harmony and agreement, a wonderful concord of minds. Pliny: When they set out, they agree together. Solinus: All share a common care for the weary, so that, if any have failed, they all gather together and lift up the exhausted ones, [col. 73] until their strength is recovered by rest. Note here the verb congruere [to come together], taken from cranes: it is properly used of cranes, and from them transferred to other things. Festus: Congruere is said from cranes, which do not separate from one another, whether they are flying or feeding. So also ingruere means to rush upon in a great host like cranes. From this it was transferred to soldiers, to rain, to hail and to other things. And in Solinus we read fluctus ingrui [waves rushing in].
Not without reason does Oppian speak of
the high-flying chorus of cranes; and Antipater of Sidon
that is, as Servius explains, flying on high. And Ausonius in the Monosyllables:
When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was the informer.
And the crane says of itself in Avienus, Fable 15:
— — — Lofty on my wing into the air I am borne, next to the stars and the gods.

For cranes fly on high, attentive to every change of the air, so as not to be overwhelmed by a storm. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, ch. 10: Εἰς ὕψος πέτονται πρὸς τὸ καθορᾶν τὰ πόῤῥω, καὶ ἐὰν ἴδωσι νέφη, καὶ χειμέρια [Eis hypsos petontai pros to kathoran ta porrhō, kai ean idōsi nephē, kai cheimeria] (Antigonus has καὶ συστροφὴν [kai systrophēn]) καταπτᾶσαι ἡσυχάζουσιν· [kataptasai hēsychazousin] They fly on high in order to see far ahead; and if they see clouds and stormy weather (or a whirlwind), they fly down and stay quiet. Accordingly it is among the signs of a coming storm when a sailor in mid-sea sees γεράνους ὑποστρεφούσας, καὶ τὴν ἔμπαλιν πετομένας [geranous hypostrephousas, kai tēn empalin petomenas], cranes turning back and flying in the opposite direction. So Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 14. You may see similar statements in Aratus, Virgil, Pliny, Theon and Avienus. But [II, 622] cranes also strive toward the greatest heights, so that from a loftier watchtower they may survey the lands they are heading for. So Solinus and Isidore. They also seem to strive for the heights because the air is calmer there, as Horus attests in these words, book 2, ch. 93: Ὑψηλῶς πάνυ ἵπτάται (γέρανος) ἵνα θεάσηται τὰ νέφη, μὴ ἄρα χειμάζῃ, ἵνα ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ διαμένῃ· [Hypsēlōs pany hiptatai (geranos) hina theasētai ta nephē, mē ara cheimazē, hina en hēsychia diamenē] The crane flies very high in order to observe the clouds, so that it may not be tossed by a storm but remain at rest. Finally, Alkazuinius gives this fourth reason: فاذا طارت ترفعت في الهوا جدا كي لا يعرض لها شي من السباع الطير [fa-idhā ṭārat taraffaʿat fī al-hawā jiddan kay lā yaʿriḍ lahā shay min al-sibāʿ al-ṭayr] And when it flies aloft, it rises very high, so that none of the birds of prey may meet it.
